name: Lena Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Prentice Electrical, a family firm in our market town. We mostly do shops and small offices: fitting out a new café, fixing the lights in the bank, the emergency lighting tests every six months for the solicitors. I like commercial work because it's tidy, the drawings are usually right and you're not in someone's bedroom. What wears me out is the early starts, because shops want you gone before they open at nine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend Marco, who drives a parcel van. My pay's on the low side, the Prentices aren't generous, and there's not many other firms round here doing commercial work. Savings, maybe two weeks' worth, since I paid off a fine Marco got last spring. We're fine month to month, but there's no slack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So nothing much changes. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never bothered with any of it anyway. At work we'd have a laugh about all the people who spent money on AI courses. I don't really post online, so probably nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thing that bothers me isn't AI, it's the high street. Three of our regular shops closed this year. Every shop on the high street that closes is a maintenance contract gone. Gordon, the owner, is handing over to his son Callum, and Callum talks about cutting the van fleet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd ask Callum straight out whether my hours are safe, because I'd rather know. And we'd stop going out on Saturdays and put that thirty quid aside instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not panicky. Just that feeling when you notice the shop next to the bakery has a 'to let' sign up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Callum said your hours might drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the emergency call-outs, because they pay time and a half. And if that wasn't enough I'd look at the agency, even though agency work is all new-build and I don't like it. I'm not going to jump ship before I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you avoid the AI tools when some people say they save time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't need them. My job's a tester, a screwdriver and the drawings. When somebody shows me something that does my work better, I'll look, but nobody has yet.

say: I'd tell people I **never bothered** with AI anyway, so nothing lost.
I'd **laugh at work** about colleagues who paid for AI courses.
think: The real threat is the **dying high street**, with three regular shops closed this year.
The owner's son talks about **cutting vans**, which worries me more than AI.
do: Carry on with **commercial maintenance** as usual.
Ask the new boss **straight out** whether her hours are safe.
Put the **Saturday night out** money, about thirty pounds, aside each week.
feel: **Uneasy** but not panicky, like noticing another 'to let' sign.
S0.quote: Every shop on the high street that closes is a maintenance contract gone.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **high street**, not technology, and she says so plainly.
She'd rather **know the truth** about her hours than guess.
She **avoids AI** because nobody has shown it does her work better.
A **handover** from father to son at the firm adds uncertainty.

steps.text: Keep doing emergency lighting tests and shop fit-outs
Ask Callum directly whether her hours are safe
Swap Saturday nights out for thirty pounds a week saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers and booking. That's Marco's depot, and the shops' tills, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be rough on some people and good for others, and there's no point pretending otherwise. At work I'd probably just get on with it. I might tell my mum not to worry about me, because nobody's making an app that rewires a café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's Marco and the shops I'm worried about. His depot already uses software for routes, and if it takes over the booking and the customer calls, there'll be fewer managers and tighter rounds. And if more shopping goes online, more shops close, and that's our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, but I'd ask Callum to put me on the bigger office refits, not the little shops. I'd cut the gym membership, forty a month. If things got really tight, we'd talk about moving back in with my parents for a year to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, more for us as a couple than for me. I can see us both earning a bit less, and with no savings, a bit less is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said office refits. Why those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if offices are changing how they work, they'll be moving desks around and putting in screens and charging points. That's work for us. Shops are just closing, offices are at least changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about moving back in with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassed, at twenty-seven. My dad would be fine about it, my mum would rearrange the whole house. But I'd rather be embarrassed for a year at my parents' house than in debt for five.

say: I'd say it's **rough on some** and good for others, no point pretending.
I'd reassure my mum that **no app rewires** a café.
think: My partner's **parcel depot** will tighten rounds once software handles bookings and calls.
More **online shopping** means more shop closures, and that's our work.
do: Ask to move onto **office refits**, which change rather than close.
Cancel the **gym membership**, saving forty a month.
Talk about **moving back** with her parents for a year if money gets tight.
feel: **Anxious** for the couple, since both incomes could dip at once.
S1.quote: I'd rather be embarrassed for a year at my parents' house than in debt for five.
fieldNote: Her own trade looks **safe**, but her partner's job and her clients don't.
She reads the market **practically**: offices change, shops just close.
Moving home is a **real option** she'd take despite the embarrassment.
With **no cushion**, even a small dip in two incomes worries her.

steps.text: Ask Callum to move her onto office refit jobs
Cancel the gym membership and save forty a month
Move back in with her parents for a year if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots three years after. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and nobody's ready, which would be true. At work everyone would be talking about it, and I'd mostly listen. I'd probably say we're tradespeople, we're the last to go, though I'm not sure I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Prentice Electrical doesn't survive this. If the shops and offices are run by AI by 2028, half of them close or shrink, and the ones left will want the cheapest contractor. Then by 2031 the robots can do the emergency lighting tests, and that's my bread and butter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, straight away. I'd move back in with Mum and Dad within six months and bank every penny. I wouldn't go chasing AI courses, I'd just keep working and wait to see which way it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit frozen. I'm not someone who changes direction easily, and this one wants me to change everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say a robot can do the lighting tests in 2031. Who would you be then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is a tester, a screwdriver and the drawings, and I can't picture who I'd be when a robot does the lighting tests. Maybe the person who fixes the robot when it falls off a ladder. Maybe nobody. That's the bit I can't picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco's job look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His van drives itself before my robot shows up, probably. So he goes first, and I'm the only wage. With two weeks of savings that lasts about as long as a bag of chips.

say: I'd say it's **mad and nobody's ready**, and mostly listen at work.
I'd claim tradespeople **go last**, without quite believing it.
think: The **family firm** likely doesn't survive as shops and offices shrink by 2028.
By 2031 robots could do **emergency lighting tests**, my bread and butter.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** immediately.
Move back in with her **parents** within six months and bank everything.
Keep working and **wait** rather than chase AI courses.
feel: **Frightened** and a bit **frozen**, because change doesn't come easily to her.
S2.quote: My job is a tester, a screwdriver and the drawings, and I can't picture who I'd be when a robot does the lighting tests.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and can't imagine what comes after.
Her partner's **delivery job** likely goes even before hers.
Her response is **defensive**: cut costs, move home, wait.
She admits being **frozen**, a candid self-read for someone resistant to change.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only
Move back in with Mum and Dad within six months
Keep working at Prentice and watch how things go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more time. Still quick though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big deal, but tradespeople have a few years, so let's not panic. I'd be the calm one at work, I think. I'd tell Marco to look at getting his electrical ticket, half joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd still lose the job eventually, maybe by 2034. The difference is I could see it coming, so I'd have a few years to save something. I'm not going to suddenly become a tech person, but I could become the person who knows the old buildings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard for three or four years, aiming for six months of rent. I'd ask the Prentices to put me through the inspection and testing course, because inspecting old buildings is about knowing the old wiring. And we'd push the move back home off, maybe forever if the savings work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. Like seeing the storm on the radar a few days out instead of it just turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could become the person who knows the old buildings. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every shop on Market Street has wiring from three different decades, and half of it isn't on any drawing. A robot works from the drawing, but I know where the cable actually goes because I've pulled it out of the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six months of rent is a big jump from two weeks. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I don't touch it, maybe. We'd stop the holiday, sell my car and share Marco's van. It would be a boring few years, but boring's fine.

say: I'd tell people tradespeople have **a few years**, so no need to panic.
I'd half-jokingly urge my partner to get an **electrical ticket**.
think: I'd probably still **lose the job** around 2034, but I'd see it coming.
I could be the person who **knows old buildings**, not a tech person.
do: Save hard toward **six months of rent** over three or four years.
Ask the firm to fund the **inspection and testing** course.
Sell her **car** and share her partner's van to save money.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, like seeing a storm days out on the radar.
S3.quote: A robot works from the drawing, but I know where the cable actually goes because I've pulled it out of the wall.
fieldNote: She still **expects to lose** her job, so worry stays high despite more time.
Her niche is **local knowledge** of old wiring that isn't on any drawing.
Extra time buys her **savings**, not reinvention.
She'd accept a **boring few years** of cutbacks to reach six months of rent.

steps.text: Save toward six months of rent over four years
Ask the Prentices to fund the inspection and testing course
Sell her car and share Marco's van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven before the AGI bit, forty or so before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so people should stop panicking. At work I'd say let's get on with the job. I'd say it to my mum too, because she'd have seen something on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably still be doing this at forty, and then something else after. I'm not sure what. Maybe the inspection work, maybe running the firm's maintenance contracts if Callum keeps it going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the inspection course over two or three years, at my own pace. I'd save a bit every month without the drama of selling the car. And honestly, I'd wait a few years before deciding anything bigger, because a lot can change in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the normal way. I already worry about the high street and money. This adds to it, it doesn't swamp it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide it's time to do something bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see a robot actually working on a real site round here, not on the news. Until then it's just talk. When I see one, I'll start moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Marco change any plans, like a house or a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about buying somewhere small in maybe five years. In this one we'd probably still try, but only if one of us has something solid. I'm not taking on a mortgage on two shaky jobs.

say: I'd tell people ten years is **plenty of time**, so stop panicking.
I'd reassure my **mum** after she'd seen it on the news.
think: I'd probably still be **doing this at forty**, with something else after.
**Inspection work** or running maintenance contracts are possible next steps.
do: Take the **inspection course** over two or three years.
Save a **little each month** without selling the car.
Hold off on **bigger decisions** until robots show up locally.
feel: **Anxious** in the normal way, added to existing money worries.
S4.quote: I'm not taking on a mortgage on two shaky jobs.
fieldNote: Her trigger to act is **seeing a robot** on a real local site.
A decade lets her **pace herself**, but money worries stay.
The couple's **house plans** hinge on one of them having secure work.
She keeps the **inspection route** in every version, a consistent plan.

steps.text: Take the inspection and testing course over three years
Save a set amount every month from wages
Hold off buying a house until one job feels solid
Wait until a robot shows up on a local site

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Marco and I would both be going at once with no money behind us. What would help is time and a bit of a cushion, like support with rent for a year while you retrain, and firms being made to pay for courses for the people they've had for years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small towns. Everything I hear is about cities and offices. Out here the shops are already closing, and nobody's talking about what happens to the people who fix them.

headlineQuote: Out here the shops are already closing, and nobody's talking about what happens to the people who fix them.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old electrician** at a family firm doing shop and office work in a market town.
She lives with her boyfriend, a parcel driver, with **two weeks** of savings after paying his fine.
She's never used AI and **sees no need**, trusting her tester, screwdriver and drawings.
Her worry starts with the **dying high street** and grows as both their jobs look exposed.
Her plan is **defensive and practical**: cut costs, move home if needed, and train in inspection.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and her partner could lose work at once with nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A year of **rent support** while people retrain.
Firms made to **pay for courses** for long-serving staff.
